session.question: How do neonatal injury models help to know about adult hearts cardiac regeneration?
session.answer:
Neonatal injury models, especially in newborn mice, are useful because the neonatal heart has a brief developmental window in which it can fully regenerate after injury, unlike the adult mammalian heart. By studying this naturally regenerative state, researchers can identify the molecular and cellular mechanisms that enable endogenous cardiomyocyte proliferation and tissue repair. These models therefore serve as in vivo systems to uncover regenerative pathways, injury-response programs, and factors that may be therapeutically activated in adult hearts, where repair is usually limited and scar formation leads to poor recovery after myocardial infarction. (costa2022neonatalinjurymodels chunk 1)

In practical terms, neonatal models help define what must change to shift an adult heart from fibrotic healing toward regeneration. The insights gained from these studies are intended to guide strategies that stimulate adult cardiac regeneration, potentially improving cardiac function after injury. (costa2022neonatalinjurymodels chunk 1)

session.context:
pqac-c3a01419: The excerpt explains that neonatal mouse hearts have a brief period of full regenerative capacity after injury, unlike adult mammalian hearts, which typically heal poorly and lead to heart failure. Because newborn mice can regenerate after cardiac injury, they serve as an in vivo model to study the molecular mechanisms that enable regeneration. These neonatal injury models help identify factors and pathways that drive endogenous cardiomyocyte proliferation and tissue repair. Insights from these studies may be used to develop therapies that could stimulate regeneration in adult hearts, where natural regenerative potential is limited.
From Alessia Costa, Sarah Cushman, Bernhard J. Haubner, Anselm A. Derda, Thomas Thum, and Christian Bär. Neonatal injury models: integral tools to decipher the molecular basis of cardiac regeneration. Basic Research in Cardiology, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00395-022-00931-w, doi:10.1007/s00395-022-00931-w.

pqac-b1ad4567: The excerpt explains that neonatal mouse heart injury models are important because newborn mice have a short developmental window in which the heart can fully regenerate after injury. These models are used to study the molecular mechanisms of cardiac regeneration and to identify factors that might stimulate endogenous cardiomyocyte proliferation in adult hearts. The paper emphasizes that such models help uncover regenerative pathways that could be translated into therapies for adult heart disease after myocardial infarction, where regeneration is normally insufficient and scar formation contributes to heart failure.
From Alessia Costa, Sarah Cushman, Bernhard J. Haubner, Anselm A. Derda, Thomas Thum, and Christian Bär. Neonatal injury models: integral tools to decipher the molecular basis of cardiac regeneration. Basic Research in Cardiology, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00395-022-00931-w, doi:10.1007/s00395-022-00931-w.

pqac-6c5953ce: The excerpt explains that after myocardial injury, endothelial cells adapt to the injured microenvironment through transcriptional and phenotypical changes, including metabolic, mesenchymal, hematopoietic, and pro-inflammatory signatures. Importantly, many of these changes are transient and endothelial cells can revert to a naïve state after injury resolves. This resilience supports repair and regeneration and helps prevent chronic dysfunction. While the excerpt does not specifically discuss neonatal injury models, it implies that studying injury responses and regenerative adaptation can reveal mechanisms of heart repair that may inform regeneration in other settings, including the adult heart.
From Lukas S. Tombor and Stefanie Dimmeler. Why is endothelial resilience key to maintain cardiac health? Basic Research in Cardiology, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00395-022-00941-8, doi:10.1007/s00395-022-00941-8.

pqac-14f22552: The excerpt is about KLF9 deficiency and inflammatory injury after myocardial infarction in adult hearts, showing that KLF9 is pro-inflammatory in macrophages and that its loss improves cardiac function and remodeling. It does not discuss neonatal injury models, cardiac regeneration, or how neonatal and adult hearts differ in regenerative capacity. Therefore, it provides little direct information for explaining how neonatal injury models help understand adult heart cardiac regeneration.
From Zhihong Chang and Hongkun Li. Klf9 deficiency protects the heart from inflammatory injury triggered by myocardial infarction.
